summary.text: Let \(L_0=4,L_1=16,L_2=63\) and \(L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\); a growth bound \(L_{n+1}\ge 3L_n\), together with the Cassini-type remainder \(\delta_n=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n\) and its recurrence \(\delta_{n+3}=4\delta_{n+1}+\delta_n\), gives \(1\le\delta_n\le L_n\). Hence \(L_{n+1}^2=L_{n+2}L_n+\delta_n\) makes the ceiling rule return exactly \(L_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the original sequence with this linear recurrence, which has the claimed generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer \(m\) satisfying
\[
\frac{m}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
Once the terms in the denominators are positive, this inequality is equivalent to
\[
m<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For any real number \(x\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(x\) is \(\lceil x\rceil-1\): this remains true when \(x\) itself is an integer, in which case the answer is \(x-1\). Hence the original rule is equivalently
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{1}
\]
For positive integers \(X,d\), one has
\[
\left\lceil\frac Xd\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{X+d-1}{d}\right\rfloor,
\]
so (1) is also the integer recurrence
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lfloor\frac{b_{n+1}^2+b_n-1}{b_n}\right\rfloor-1.
\tag{2}
\]
We shall prove that this nonlinear recurrence is obeyed by the linear recurrence associated with the conjectured generating function.

Define a sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
L_0=4,\qquad L_1=16,\qquad L_2=63,
\tag{3}
\]
and
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{4}
\]
We first establish some growth facts which, in particular, show that the subtraction in (4) always gives a positive integer.

We claim that
\[
L_{n+1}\ge 3L_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{5}
\]
The first two cases are immediate:
\[
L_1=16\ge 12=3L_0,
\qquad
L_2=63\ge48=3L_1.
\]
For the induction step, suppose the assertion has already been proved at all earlier indices. In particular,
\[
L_{n+1}\ge3L_n,
\qquad
L_{n+2}\ge3L_{n+1}.
\]
These inequalities imply \(L_{n+2}\ge L_n\). Therefore, using (4),
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n
          \ge4L_{n+2}-L_{n+2}
          =3L_{n+2}.
\]
This proves (5) by strong induction. It also justifies ordinary integer subtraction in (4), since \(L_n\le L_{n+2}<4L_{n+2}\). Starting from \(L_0>0\), (5) shows that every \(L_n\) is positive. It also shows that the sequence is increasing, in the weak sense \(L_n\le L_{n+1}\).

The central ingredient is a Cassini-type determinant. Define
\[
\Delta_n=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n.
\tag{6}
\]
We will prove the sharp-enough bounds
\[
1\le \Delta_n\le L_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{7}
\]
First compute the initial values. From (4),
\[
L_3=4L_2-L_0=4\cdot63-4=248,
\]
and
\[
L_4=4L_3-L_1=4\cdot248-16=976.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\Delta_0=16^2-63\cdot4=256-252=4,
\]
\[
\Delta_1=63^2-248\cdot16=3969-3968=1,
\]
and
\[
\Delta_2=248^2-976\cdot63=61504-61488=16.
\]
Thus (7) holds for \(n=0,1,2\), because respectively
\[
1\le4\le4,\qquad 1\le1\le16,\qquad 1\le16\le63.
\]

We next derive a recurrence for \(\Delta_n\). We claim that
\[
\Delta_{n+3}=4\Delta_{n+1}+\Delta_n.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, recurrence (4), at three successive indices, gives
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n,
\]
\[
L_{n+4}=4L_{n+3}-L_{n+1},
\]
\[
L_{n+5}=4L_{n+4}-L_{n+2}.
\]
Substituting these into
\[
\Delta_{n+3}=L_{n+4}^2-L_{n+5}L_{n+3}
\]
and expanding gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{n+3}
&=L_{n+4}^2-(4L_{n+4}-L_{n+2})L_{n+3}\\
&=L_{n+4}(L_{n+4}-4L_{n+3})+L_{n+2}L_{n+3}\\
&=-L_{n+1}L_{n+4}+L_{n+2}L_{n+3}\\
&=-L_{n+1}(4L_{n+3}-L_{n+1})+L_{n+2}L_{n+3}\\
&=L_{n+1}^2+(L_{n+2}-4L_{n+1})L_{n+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4\Delta_{n+1}+\Delta_n
&=4(L_{n+2}^2-L_{n+3}L_{n+1})
 +(L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n)\\
&=L_{n+1}^2-4L_{n+1}L_{n+3}
  +L_{n+2}(4L_{n+2}-L_n)\\
&=L_{n+1}^2-4L_{n+1}L_{n+3}+L_{n+2}L_{n+3},
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(4L_{n+2}-L_n=L_{n+3}\). This is the same expression, proving (8).

We now prove (7) by strong induction. Suppose the bounds are known for \(\Delta_n\) and \(\Delta_{n+1}\). By (8),
\[
\Delta_{n+3}=4\Delta_{n+1}+\Delta_n.
\]
Both terms on the right are positive, so \(\Delta_{n+3}>0\), and since it is an integer this means \(\Delta_{n+3}\ge1\).

For the upper bound, the induction hypotheses give
\[
\Delta_n\le L_n,
\qquad
\Delta_{n+1}\le L_{n+1},
\]
and hence
\[
\Delta_{n+3}\le4L_{n+1}+L_n.
\tag{9}
\]
We compare the right side with \(L_{n+3}\). From the growth estimate (5),
\[
L_{n+2}\ge3L_{n+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
L_{n+1}\ge3L_n.
\]
In particular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4L_{n+2}-L_n-(4L_{n+1}+L_n)
&=4(L_{n+2}-L_{n+1})-2L_n\\
&\ge 8L_{n+1}-2L_n\\
&\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
4L_{n+1}+L_n\le4L_{n+2}-L_n=L_{n+3}.
\]
Together with (9), this proves \(\Delta_{n+3}\le L_{n+3}\). The three initial cases and this induction establish (7) for every \(n\ge0\).

We can now show that \(L_n\) satisfies the nonlinear ceiling recurrence. From the definition of \(\Delta_n\),
\[
L_{n+1}^2=L_{n+2}L_n+\Delta_n.
\tag{10}
\]
By (7),
\[
1\le\Delta_n\le L_n.
\tag{11}
\]
Since \(L_n>0\), equations (10) and (11) yield
\[
\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}
 =L_{n+2}+\frac{\Delta_n}{L_n},
\qquad
0<\frac{\Delta_n}{L_n}\le1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil=L_{n+2}+1,
\]
including the endpoint case \(\Delta_n=L_n\), when the displayed quotient is exactly \(L_{n+2}+1\). Hence
\[
L_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{12}
\]
Equivalently, in the integer-division form used in (2),
\[
L_{n+2}
=\left\lfloor\frac{L_{n+1}^2+L_n-1}{L_n}\right\rfloor-1.
\tag{13}
\]
For completeness, (13) can also be seen directly from (10):
\[
L_{n+1}^2+L_n-1
=(L_{n+2}+1)L_n+(\Delta_n-1).
\]
By (11), the remainder satisfies
\[
0\le\Delta_n-1<L_n,
\]
so division by \(L_n\) has quotient exactly \(L_{n+2}+1\), and subtracting one gives \(L_{n+2}\).

We now identify the original sequence with \(L\). We prove
\[
b_n=L_n\qquad(n\ge0)
\tag{14}
\]
by strong induction. At \(n=0,1\), this follows from the common initial values
\[
b_0=L_0=4,
\qquad
b_1=L_1=16.
\]
Suppose the equality has been established through indices \(n+1\). Applying the original recurrence (1), then the induction hypothesis, and finally (12), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+2}
&=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1\\
&=\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1\\
&=L_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This also shows inductively that all original-sequence terms are positive, so every ratio and every division used in its definition is legitimate. Thus (14) holds for all \(n\).

It follows immediately from (3), (4), and (14) that
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}.
\tag{15}
\]
This is precisely the stated linear-recurrence form of the conjecture. In the piecewise formulation, the cases \(n=0,1,2\) give \(4,16,63\), respectively, while writing \(n=k+3\) in every remaining case turns (4) into
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}.
\]

Finally, we verify explicitly that (15) is equivalent to the conjectured generating function. Let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)
\]
is, for \(n\ge3\),
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3},
\]
which vanishes by (15). The coefficients in degrees \(0,1,2\) are respectively
\[
b_0=4,
\]
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,
\]
and
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2,
\]
and hence, as an identity of formal power series,
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence defined by the original strict extremal-ratio rule has exactly the conjectured generating function.
